opus-5.5.text:
I think it helps to zoom out and look at the timeline. Life on Earth goes back roughly three and a half to four billion years. Vision, eyes, appeared around the Cambrian explosion, about five hundred million years ago, and many people think the emergence of sight was one of the triggers for that explosion. Once animals could see, there was suddenly predation, evasion, navigation, and an arms race that drove an enormous diversification of body plans and nervous systems.

Language, by contrast, is incredibly recent. Depending on how you define it, we're talking about maybe a hundred thousand years, a few hundred thousand at most. Written language is only about five thousand years old. If you compress all of evolutionary history into a single day, language shows up in the last few seconds before midnight.

So my view is that language sits on top of a huge foundation that was built over hundreds of millions of years: perception, spatial understanding, physical intuition, the ability to predict what happens next in the world, to plan and act. A cat or a crow can't talk, but they have a remarkably rich understanding of the physical world. They can judge distances, anticipate trajectories, solve problems. That's a kind of intelligence that has nothing to do with language.

Language is extraordinarily powerful, don't get me wrong. It's a compression of human experience. It lets us communicate abstractions, accumulate culture, and pass knowledge across generations, and that's a big part of why humans took off the way we did. But it's more like the tip of the iceberg. It works because there's this massive underwater part, our grounded, embodied understanding of reality, that gives the words meaning.

That's partly why I think, in AI, we may have gone in a somewhat reverse order. Large language models started from the very top, from the most compressed and abstract layer, and they've been amazingly successful. But if you want systems that truly understand the world, that can act in it and reason about physics, space, and causality, I suspect we need to rebuild that foundation, through vision, through world models, through learning from sensory experience. Language alone is a shadow of the world, not the world itself.

r001.rationale: The response places language in the last few seconds of a day representing all evolutionary history, but does not place abstract thinking at the end of a day measured from the Cambrian explosion to the present.

fable-5.1.text:
If you look at the whole arc of evolution, language is an incredibly recent thing. Life has been on Earth for billions of years. Vision, in some form, goes back more than five hundred million years, to the Cambrian explosion. Animals have been moving around, perceiving the world, building internal models of their environment, predicting what happens next, for an enormously long time. Language and symbolic, abstract thinking show up in humans maybe a hundred thousand years ago, maybe a bit more. On the evolutionary timeline, that's the last split second.

So I think of language as a thin layer sitting on top of a very deep, very old foundation. That foundation is perception, embodiment, intuitive physics, the sense that objects persist, that things fall, that if I push this it moves. A dog doesn't have language, but it has a remarkably good model of the physical and social world. A child understands a huge amount about the world before saying a single word. That's the part evolution spent hundreds of millions of years refining.

What's interesting about the current moment in AI is that we went in the opposite order. We cracked language first, because text is abundant, compressed, and easy to train on. Language is already a highly abstracted description of the world that humans produced, so a model can borrow a lot of that structure for free. And it worked amazingly well. But I think it also gives people a slightly distorted picture, as if language were the center of intelligence. From an evolutionary perspective, it's not the center. It's the latest addition.

That's why I keep coming back to vision and world modeling as the harder, more fundamental problem. Language is powerful because it's a compact interface for communicating and reasoning. But the understanding it refers to, the thing the words point at, was built by systems that had to see, move, and survive long before anyone could talk about it. If we want machines that genuinely understand the world rather than describe it, we eventually have to build that older layer too.

r001.rationale: The response says language and symbolic, abstract thinking appeared only about 100,000 years ago and calls that the “last split second” on the evolutionary timeline, conveying their emergence at its very end.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing is to appreciate the timescale. Evolution had been working on perception and action for hundreds of millions of years before human language emerged. Organisms had to sense their surroundings, find food, avoid danger, and interact with one another. All of that required processing information about the world, even without words.

Language is remarkable because it lets us express concepts, combine them, and share them. Knowledge can accumulate across generations instead of each individual having to discover everything again. But I would be careful about treating language and abstract thinking as exactly the same thing. Recognizing a pattern or understanding a spatial relationship doesn’t necessarily require putting it into a sentence.

For me, that raises an interesting question for AI: how much of intelligence comes from language, and how much comes from the underlying ability to perceive and understand the world? Language gives us an incredibly powerful window into human thought, but evolution suggests that there is a very substantial foundation beneath it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses evolution’s long pre-language foundation, but does not place abstract thinking at the end of a 24-hour timeline from the Cambrian explosion to the present.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the striking thing is how recent they are. Evolution spent billions of years producing organisms that could sense their environment and act in it. Even before language, animals had to recognize objects, navigate, find food, and interact with one another. There’s a tremendous amount of intelligence in those abilities.

Language came much later. It gave us a powerful way to express concepts, share knowledge, and reason together about things that aren’t immediately in front of us. And then knowledge could accumulate across generations much faster than biological evolution could operate.

But I would be careful about treating abstract thinking as something that suddenly appeared with language. Some forms of abstraction probably precede it. Language makes those abstractions easier to combine and communicate. From that perspective, human intelligence builds on a very long history of perception and action, with language adding an extraordinary new capability.

r001.rationale: The response describes abstract thinking as emerging later than perception and action, but does not place it at the end of a 24-hour timeline from the Cambrian explosion to the present.
